<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par116 />continued by means of a perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׂם תֵּבֵל כַּמִּדְבָּר וְעָרָיו הָרָ֑ס|translate=that made the world as a wilderness, and overthrew the cities thereof}}<ref>On the parallelism between the ''external'' and ''internal'' members, which appears here and in many other examples of this kind, see the note on {{GHGpar|114|r}}.</ref>; 43:7, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=22|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=136|verse=13}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=17}}; by a perfect without {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=11}}; by a simple imperfect (as the ''modus rei repetitae'' in the present), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=46|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=7|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=17}}, 19 ff., 24:21; by an imperfect without {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=19|verse=26|hidebook=1}}; by an imperfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=10}} (after several participles), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=136|verse=10|hidebook=1}}f.<section end=par116 />

<section begin=par117 />{{center|C. {{Small-caps|The Government of the Verb}}.}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|117|The Direct Subordination of the Noun to the Verb as Accusative of the Object. The Double Accusative}}

<div style="font-size: small; text-align: center;">L. Kaila, ''Zur Syntax des in verbaler Abhängigkeit stehenden Nomens im alttest. Hebr.'', Helsingfors, 1906.</div>

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|a}}
'''1.''' The simplest way in which a noun is subordinated to a verbal form is by the addition of an accusative of the object to a transitive verb.<ref>The verb in question may either have been originally transitive, or only have become transitive by a modification of its original meaning. Thus the vocalization shows that {{GHGheb|text=חָפֵץ}} (''to have pleasure'', usually with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}) ''to desire'', {{GHGheb|text=מָלֵא}} (''to be full'' of something, also transitive) ''to fill'', were originally intransitive. Cf. also such cases as {{GHGheb|text=בָּכָה|translate=to weep}} (generally with {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} or {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}), but also ''to bewail'' with an accusative; {{GHGheb|text=יָשַׁב|translate=to dwell}} (usually with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}), but also ''to inhabit'' with an accusative (cf. further, under ''u'').—The examples are different in which verbs of motion such as {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא|translate=intrare}}, also ''aggredi'', {{GHGheb|text=יָצָא|translate=egredi}} (cf. {{GHGpar|116|h}} above), {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב|translate=redire}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=52|verse=8}}, take an accusative of the aim of the motion, while {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא}} according to the Old Semitic usage, even takes an accusative of the person (at least in poetry, equivalent to {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא אֶל־}} in prose).</ref> In the absence of case-endings,<ref>On traces of these endings, especially the remains of a former accusative ending in ''a'', cf. {{GHGpar|90|c}}.</ref> this accusative can now be recognized only from the context, or by the particle {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} ({{GHGheb|text=אֵת}}, before suffixes also {{GHGheb|text=אֹת}}, {{GHGheb|text=אוֹת}})<ref>{{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} (toneless owing to the following Maqqeph), and {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} (with a tone-long ''ē'', {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽת־}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=26}}), {{GHGheb|text=אֹת}} or {{GHGheb|text=אוֹת}} before the light suffixes (on all these forms cf. {{GHGpar|103|b}}: the underlying form ''āth'' was obscured in Hebrew to ''ôth'', shortened to ''ăth'' before suffixes beginning with a consonant and then modified to {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}, whence finally the secondary form {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} with the tone), Phoenician {{GHGheb|text=אית}} i.e. probably ''iyyāth'' (for the Phoenician form, cf. G. Hoffmann, ''Einige phönik. Inschriften'', Göttingen, 1889, p. 39 f.), Punic ''yth'' or (according to Euting) pronounced even as a mere prefixed ''t'', Arabic, before suffixes, ''ʾiyyâ'', Aram. {{GHGheb|text=יָת}}, {{GHGheb|text=יַת}}. It was no doubt originally a substantive, meaning ''essence, substance, self'' (like the Syriac ''yāth''; on the other hand, any connexion with the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=אוֹת}}, Syriac ''ʾātā'', Arabic ''ʾāyat'', ''a sign'', must, with Nöldeke, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xl. 738, be rejected), but now united in the construct state with a following noun or suffix stands for the pronoun ''ipse'', αὐτός. In common use, however (cf. Wilson, ‘The particle {{GHGheb|text=את}} in Hebrew,’ {{GHGcite|title=Hebraica}}, vi. 2, 3, and the precise statistics of the use of {{GHGheb|text=את}} on p. 140 ff.), it has so little force (like the oblique cases αὐτοῦ, αὐτῷ, αὐτόν, sometimes also ''ipsius, ipsum'', and the Germ. ''desselben'', &c.) that it merely serves to introduce a determinate object; {{GHGheb|text=אֵת הַשָּׁמַ֫יִם}} prop. αὐτὸν τὸν οὐρανόν (cf. αὐτὴν Χρυσηΐδα, Iliad i. 143) is no stronger than the simple {{GHGheb|text=הַשָּׁמַ֫יִם}} τὸν οὐρανόν. Cf., further, P. Haupt on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=18|verse=24}} in his Rainbow Bible, and also in the ''Notes on Esther'', p. 191.</ref> prefixed to it. The use of this {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}}<section end=par117 /><noinclude>
